title: Indian Seafarer Killed as Cargo Vessel Al Jusufi Is Struck off Oman
excerpt: The Indian-flagged MSV Al Jusufi, sailing from Hamriyah to Porbandar with 14 Indian crew, was hit by an unidentified aerial object on November 2. Gandhar Nahim Ajij, 26, of Gujarat died of his injuries; 13 crewmates were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard.
body:
• The Indian-flagged vessel MSV Al Jusufi, carrying 14 Indian seafarers, was struck by an unidentified aerial object near the coast of Oman on November 2, Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said.
  • Gandhar Nahim Ajij, a 26-year-old seafarer from Salaya in Gujarat's Devbhumi Dwarka district, succumbed to his injuries while being taken to a hospital at Khasab Port.
  • The other 13 crew members abandoned the vessel in a liferaft and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard.
  • The Shipping Ministry and the Indian Embassy in Oman are coordinating assistance and the repatriation of the survivors and of Ajij's mortal remains; no source for the object has been identified.

An Indian seafarer was killed when the Indian-flagged cargo vessel MSV Al Jusufi was struck by an unidentified aerial object while navigating near the coast of Oman on Monday, November 2. The vessel was carrying 14 Indian seafarers. Thirteen of them evacuated safely and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard; one did not survive his injuries.

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal confirmed the death in a post on X on Tuesday. The deceased seafarer was identified as Gandhar Nahim Ajij, a 26-year-old resident of Salaya in Gujarat's Devbhumi Dwarka district. According to the minister's account, the vessel was struck at around 4 p.m. on Monday; all 14 crew members abandoned the damaged vessel and escaped in a liferaft, and Ajij succumbed to his injuries while being transported to a hospital at Khasab Port.

"While 13 crew members safely evacuated and were rescued by the Omani Coast Guard, I am deeply saddened to report that one of seafarer, Gandhar Nahim Ajij from Gujarat, tragically succumbed to his injuries."

— Sarbananda Sonowal, Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways

The Voyage and the Official Response

A report by the Directorate of Maritime Administration stated that Al Jusufi had departed Hamriyah Port in the United Arab Emirates on October 31, bound for Porbandar in Gujarat, with 14 Indian crew members on board. Sonowal said the Shipping Ministry and the Indian Embassy in Oman are in contact with local authorities to ensure immediate assistance for the 13 survivors and to facilitate the swift repatriation of the surviving crew members and the mortal remains of the deceased seafarer. The embassy is coordinating with local authorities on the early return of the rescued crew.

The Ministry of External Affairs expressed condolences to Ajij's family and raised concerns over repeated attacks on commercial vessels in West Asia, calling for an immediate reduction in regional tensions and for attacks on commercial shipping and civilian infrastructure to stop, with safe and unrestricted navigation through international waterways ensured in accordance with international law.

What Is Not Yet Known

No authority has identified the aerial object that struck the vessel or who was responsible for it. Officials have described it only as unidentified, and the available statements do not establish whether the vessel was deliberately targeted. Those questions remain open while the survivors are assisted and repatriation is arranged.

A Pattern Indian Seafarers Are Sailing Through

The incident comes amid continuing maritime security concerns linked to the ongoing West Asia conflict. According to the figures cited in the reports, 23 Indians have lost their lives in the conflict so far, including 15 seafarers, and several other Indian sailors have been reported missing following attacks on commercial vessels. India has more than 3.2 lakh seafarers — the second-largest seafaring workforce globally after the Philippines — and more than 18,000 Indian seafarers are currently serving on vessels operating in the West Asia region. For the families of those crews, the Al Jusufi strike is not an isolated headline but the latest in a series of attacks that have reached Indian-flagged and Indian-crewed shipping.
